column1:
• Students will be able to convert a negative binary floating-point number into denary using two's complement
• Students will be able to complete Activity 13F across positive and negative examples
column2:
• Students will be able to convert a positive denary number into binary floating-point representation using both methods
• Students will be able to represent fractional denary values in binary floating-point format
column3:
• Students will be able to convert a negative denary number into binary floating-point representation
• Students will be able to apply two's complement to the integer part before converting to floating-point format
column4:
• Students will be able to explain what normalisation is and why it is needed
• Students will be able to normalise a binary floating-point number by shifting the mantissa and adjusting the exponent
column5:
• Students will be able to explain overflow, underflow and rounding errors in floating-point representation
• Students will be able to evaluate the trade-off between precision (mantissa size) and range (exponent size)

column1:
• Recap: two volunteers demonstrate their Activity 13F solutions on the board — class checks and corrects
• Teacher-led worked examples: Examples 13.3 and 13.4 (negative mantissa values) — demonstrating two's complement conversion of the mantissa before applying Method 2
• Paired practice: Activity 13F parts f–j (negative values) — students work in pairs, comparing answers and identifying errors
column2:
• Teacher-led worked examples: Example 13.5 (+4.5) and Example 13.6 (+0.171875) using both Method 1 (improper fraction) and Method 2 (binary conversion then binary point shift)
• Class discussion: why must the mantissa start with 0.1 for a positive normalised number? (preview of normalisation)
• Individual practice: Activity 13G Q2 parts a–e (convert positive denary numbers +3.5, 0.3125, 15.375, 41/64, 9.125 into binary floating-point)
column3:
• Recap: quick-fire check — how do you convert a positive denary number to binary floating-point? (3-step summary on the board)
• Teacher-led worked example: Example 13.7 (−10.375) using both methods — emphasising the two's complement step in Method 2 and the 1.0 mantissa format for negative numbers
• Individual practice: Activity 13G Q2 parts f–j (negative denary conversions: −15/32, −3.5, −10.25, −1.046875, −3 11/32)
column4:
• Starter: show Figure 13.8 from the textbook — four different representations of the number 2. Class discussion: why is this a problem? What rule could fix it?
• Teacher-led explanation of normalisation rules: positive numbers must start 0.1, negative numbers must start 1.0; shift bits left, reduce exponent by the number of shifts
• Worked examples: Examples 13.8 and 13.9 on the board (positive and negative normalisation), then students complete Activity 13H (normalise 10 floating-point numbers)
column5:
• Teacher-led explanation using the 5.88 rounding example from section 13.3 — step-by-step binary approximation; result is stored as 5.75; discuss how extending the mantissa reduces error
• Class discussion of overflow (result too large for word size) and underflow (result too small) using Activity 13I Q3 scenarios; introduce the special case of representing zero
• Precision vs range: analyse Figures 13.10–13.16 — compare 12-bit mantissa/4-bit exponent vs 4-bit mantissa/12-bit exponent; Activity 13I Q1, Q2 and Q4

column1: Cold-call Q&A: if the mantissa starts with a 1 bit, what does this indicate? Walk through the steps to convert a negative mantissa — what must you do before shifting the binary point?
column2: Students check each other's answers for Activity 13G Q2 a–e and identify any steps where errors were made — teacher addresses common mistakes
column3: Exit ticket: convert −6.5 into binary floating-point format (8-bit mantissa, 8-bit exponent) showing all steps — teacher marks on entry next lesson
column4: Traffic light self-assessment against the two LOs. Common error discussion: what happens to the exponent when you shift the mantissa left by 3 places?
column5: End-of-chapter exam question 1 (parts a i, a ii) — students attempt under timed conditions (12 minutes), then peer-mark using class discussion

column1: Activity 13F parts f–j if not completed in class. Write a step-by-step guide in your own words for converting a negative binary floating-point number into denary
column2: Activity 13G Q1 parts a–e — convert the given fractions with exponents into binary floating-point format. Show all working clearly
column3: Activity 13G Q1 parts f–j — convert negative fraction × exponent values into binary floating-point. Then attempt Extension Activity 13C: show why two given representations are equivalent
column4: Complete any remaining questions from Activity 13H. Write a brief explanation of why normalisation improves precision. Attempt Extension Activity 13F: how is zero represented in normalised floating-point? Research and explain
column5: Complete end-of-chapter question 1 in full. Write a paragraph evaluating: if a computer doubles its mantissa size from 16 to 32 bits but keeps the same total word length, what are the consequences for precision and range?
